title: How can communities respond to environmental change?
essentialQuestion: What can people do when their environment changes?
learningGoal: Compare ways a community can respond to environmental change, using evidence about safety and fairness.

warmUp.question: When a path becomes hard to use, who should help decide what to do?

evidence.label: Fictional example created for this lesson.
evidence.question: What does each idea do well? Who might it leave out?

cards.title: Brookside: the problem
items: A low footbridge crosses a small river in Brookside.
In recent years, heavier rain has sometimes covered the bridge with water.
Children cross the bridge to get to school, and traders cross it to get to the market.
The bridge has steps at both ends.

cards.title: Three ideas for the Brookside footbridge

cases.name: Idea A: a warning sign
cases.body: Put a sign by the bridge: 'Do not cross when water covers the bridge.' It is cheap and quick.

cases.name: Idea B: raise the bridge
cases.body: Build the bridge higher, above the water, and add a ramp instead of steps. It costs more and takes months.

cases.name: Idea C: share warnings
cases.body: Send phone messages when heavy rain is coming, and put printed notices at the market and the school, in several languages.

sections.heading: Environments can change
sections.text: The environment is everything around us: land, water, air, plants and animals. Environments change over time. As the climate changes, some places now get heavier rain, while others have longer dry seasons. People change places too. For example, when many trees are cut down on a hillside, heavy rain can wash the soil away more easily, because there are no roots to hold it. In Brookside, heavier rain now sometimes covers the low footbridge. Children use the bridge to reach school, and traders use it to reach the market. The community needs a plan.
sections.simpler: The environment is everything around us. It is land, water, air, plants and animals. The environment can change. Some places get more rain now. Other places get less rain. People change places too. Tree roots hold soil on hills. If people cut the trees, rain can wash the soil away. In Brookside, heavy rain sometimes covers a low bridge. Children use it to go to school. The town needs a plan.

sections.heading: Communities find ways to adapt
sections.text: Around the world, communities adapt to changes in their environment. In Bangladesh, many fields stay under water for months in the rainy season. Some farmers build floating gardens from water plants and grow vegetables on top. In Africa, countries from Senegal to Djibouti are working on the Great Green Wall. They plant trees and care for the land to stop it from turning into desert. On many coasts in Asia, people plant mangrove trees, whose roots help protect the shore from waves. Each of these is a response that fits the local place.
sections.simpler: Communities around the world adapt. In Bangladesh, many fields are under water in the rainy season. So some farmers make gardens that float. They grow vegetables on top. In Africa, many countries plant trees across a wide, dry area. The trees help stop the land from turning into desert. In parts of Asia, people plant trees by the sea. The roots help keep the land safe from waves. Each response fits its place.

sections.heading: A good plan includes everyone
sections.text: A response only works if people can use it. Look at the three ideas for Brookside. A warning sign is quick, but it does not make the bridge safer, and some people cannot read it. Raising the bridge lowers the risk, and a ramp helps people who use wheelchairs or push carts. Phone alerts can warn people early, but not everyone has a phone or data. Printed notices at the market reach more people. Making sure that everyone can use a plan is called inclusion. Often, two ideas together work better than one, and it helps to ask the people who use the bridge.
sections.simpler: A plan only works if people can use it. A sign is quick. But it does not make the bridge safe. A higher bridge is safer. A ramp helps people who cannot use steps. A phone alert warns people early. But not everyone has a phone. Paper notices at the market help too. When everyone can use a plan, that is called inclusion. Two ideas together can work better than one.

glossary.definition: The land, water, air, plants and animals around us.
glossary.example: In Brookside, the environment changed when the rain got heavier.

glossary.definition: To change what you do so it fits new conditions.
glossary.example: Some farmers in Bangladesh adapt by growing vegetables on floating gardens.

glossary.definition: Something people do to deal with a problem.
glossary.example: Raising the bridge is one response to heavier rain in Brookside.

glossary.definition: A message that warns people about danger.
glossary.example: A phone alert can tell people in Brookside that heavy rain is coming.

glossary.definition: Making sure everyone can take part and get help.
glossary.example: Adding a ramp to the Brookside bridge is an example of inclusion.

checks.question: Which idea changes the bridge itself to make it safer?

options.text: Putting a warning sign by the bridge
options.feedback: Not quite. A sign warns people, but the bridge stays the same. Look for an idea that changes the bridge.
Not quite. Notices share news, but the bridge stays the same. Look for an idea that changes the bridge.

options.text: Raising the bridge with a ramp
options.feedback: Yes. A higher bridge stays above the water, and a ramp helps more people cross.

checks.question: Why should Brookside use printed notices as well as phone alerts?

options.text: Some people do not have a phone or data.
options.feedback: Yes. Phone alerts miss people with no phone or data. Printed notices reach more people.

options.text: Paper notices can stop the rain.
options.feedback: Not quite. Paper cannot stop rain. The lesson says notices help people who do not get phone alerts.

options.text: Everyone in Brookside has the same phone.
options.feedback: Not quite. People do not all have a phone or data. Read the part about a good plan again.

checks.question: What should Brookside ask the people who use the bridge before it chooses a plan?
checks.placeholder: Think about who crosses the bridge, when, and what makes it hard...

write.prompt: Choose two of the ideas for Brookside to use together. Explain how they make the crossing safer and how they include more people.
sentenceStarters: I would use idea ___ and idea ___ together.
This makes the crossing safer because...
One thing I would still ask people is...
selfCheck: I explained how they make the crossing safer.
I explained how they include more people.
write.example: I would use idea B and idea C together. This makes the crossing safer because the new bridge will stay above the water. The ramp also helps people who use wheelchairs or push carts. It includes more people because phone alerts and paper notices can reach people with and without phones. One thing I would still ask people is which languages to use on the notices.

speak.partnerTask: Choose a role: a student, a market trader with a cart, or an older person. Tell your partner one worry about one of the ideas.
speak.independentTask: Give a 30-second recommendation that starts with 'A fair response should...'

watch.title: UNICEF Disability and Climate Change
watch.why: It shows why people with disabilities must be part of planning for heavy rain and other changes in the environment.
watch.beforeQuestion: Why should the people who face a risk help plan the response?
watch.afterQuestion: What is one thing that could make a warning or a safe route hard for some people to use?
watch.summary: In this short UNICEF video, people talk about climate change and disability. Heavy rain, landslides and storms can cause problems for a whole town. But the video says these events are even harder for children with disabilities. Not every child can hear a warning sound. Not every child can run to a safe place. So these children need different plans. The main message is to make these plans together, before danger comes. Ask people with disabilities, because they know what they need. The video asks for warnings that work for all, a safe path for all, and safe places that all can use. When you plan for everyone from the start, the plan is better for all.
keyPoints: Heavy rain and landslides affect whole communities, and some people face extra barriers.
People with disabilities know what they need and should help plan responses.
Planning for everyone from the start makes a response stronger.
watch.contentNote: People in the video talk about dangerous rainfall and landslides. Preview it first. Learners can read the written summary instead, and no one should be asked about disasters they have lived through.

reflect.completionMessage: You finished Lesson 14. You compared ways a community can respond to change, thinking about safety and fairness.

visual.description: A side-by-side picture of the fictional Brookside footbridge. On the left, the old low bridge has steps at each end, and the river water has just reached its surface after rain. On the right, the new bridge sits well above the water, with a gentle ramp at one end. A person pushing a market cart and a person using a wheelchair are crossing it. At the market end, a small notice board shows a printed rain notice.
visual.alt: Illustration comparing a low footbridge with steps near high water and a raised footbridge with a ramp that people with carts and wheelchairs can use.

educatorNotes: Floods, landslides and extreme weather may be hard topics for learners who have lived through them. Keep the focus on how communities plan and prepare, don't ask learners about disasters they experienced, and let anyone step out of the discussion.
Preview the UNICEF video: people discuss dangerous rainfall and landslides. The written summary can replace it.
Brookside is fictional. You could add a real local example of preparation, such as a school's rain-day plan or a community notice board.
The speaking roles ask learners to imagine other people's needs. Keep them respectful; learners never need to share their own needs or disabilities.
changes: Expanded the 101-word reading to three sections: how environments change, real adaptations, and fair plans.
Added real examples: floating gardens in Bangladesh, the Great Green Wall across Africa, and mangrove planting on Asian coasts.
Named the fictional place 'Brookside' and turned the list card into a problem card plus a cases card for the three ideas.
Glossary: kept response, alert and inclusion; replaced resilience with environment and adapt. Every word now appears in both text and simpler.
Rewrote simpler English at about grade 3; correct answers now sit third and first.
Kept the video, moved its Base44 warning into contentNote and wrote a stand-alone summary.
